opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there are a few things going on there. First of all, the assumption that getting from AGI to superintelligence requires just scaling up the same kind of hardware and training ever bigger models of the same kind is, I think, probably wrong. If you have a genuinely human-level AGI, and I mean one that can do science and engineering and math at the level of a strong human researcher, then the first thing it's going to do, or the first thing we're going to ask it to do, is to improve its own algorithms. And there's an enormous amount of slack in the algorithms we're using now. Current deep neural nets are incredibly wasteful. The human brain runs on something like twenty watts, and we're burning gigawatts training these models. So there's many orders of magnitude of efficiency gain sitting there to be found by better software, better cognitive architectures, better learning algorithms, without needing to build a single new fab.

Then second, an AGI that's actually at human level can copy itself. You don't have one Einstein, you have a thousand or a million of them running in parallel on whatever compute you already have, working twenty-four hours a day, not getting tired, sharing knowledge directly with each other. So even on a fixed hardware base, the amount of research effort going into making the next system smarter jumps enormously.

And third, even where you do hit physical bottlenecks, chip design, materials science, manufacturing processes, these are exactly the sorts of things a smart AGI can help speed up. It can design better chips, it can optimize the fab processes, it can figure out new computing substrates. Sure, there's some irreducible latency in the physical world. You can't build a fab overnight. But you're talking maybe months or a few years, not decades.

So my intuition has been for a long time that once you get to a real human-level AGI, the transition to something massively superhuman is likely to be fairly fast, maybe a few years. I don't think the physical constraints buy you much of a buffer there. Which is one reason I think it matters so much how we get to that first AGI, who controls it, what values it's oriented toward, whether it's developed in an open and decentralized way rather than by one company or one government. Because you may not get a long, leisurely period to course-correct after that point.

r001.rationale: The response discusses algorithmic efficiency and hardware needs, but does not claim human-level AGI would require less training data than modern LLMs.

r002.rationale: It says human-level AGI could improve its algorithms and that better software, architectures, and learning algorithms could yield major gains without new fabs, supporting a software self-optimization path.

r003.rationale: It mentions better software, cognitive architectures, and learning algorithms, but does not identify rebuilding the software stack from the ground up.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that the physical requirements are only a bottleneck if you assume the path from AGI to superintelligence runs primarily through scaling up the same kind of hardware and the same kind of training runs we're doing now. And I don't think that's the right assumption.

Once you have a system at human level, a genuine AGI that can do the work of a competent AI researcher or a competent chip designer, the game changes qualitatively. The thing that's expensive right now is that humans are the ones doing the thinking about how to make these systems better, and humans are slow and there aren't that many of them with the right skills. An AGI can be copied. You can have a thousand or a million instances working on algorithmic improvements, on more efficient architectures, on better learning methods that don't need to see the whole internet five times to learn a concept.

And there's a lot of room there. The human brain runs on about twenty watts. Current large models are wildly inefficient compared to that, both in training and inference. So there's clearly a huge amount of algorithmic headroom that doesn't require building more fabs or buying more GPUs. It requires better ideas, and better ideas are exactly what a human-level AI system, running at scale, can produce.

Now, I'll grant that some of these improvements, if they're really radical, might want new kinds of hardware, neuromorphic chips or whatever. And yes, building new fabs takes years. But even there, an AGI would accelerate the design and the engineering, and in the meantime it could squeeze a lot more out of the hardware that already exists. There are enormous amounts of compute sitting around in data centers that could be used far more efficiently with better software.

So my view is that physical constraints are real, but they bound the rate of one particular path, and they bound it much less tightly than people assume once you factor in that the AGI itself is doing the research. It won't be instantaneous. Maybe it's a few years rather than a few months. But in the scheme of things, a few years from AGI to superintelligence is still extraordinarily fast, and it's not the sort of thing that gives you a comfortable decade to get your governance in order.

r001.rationale: It says improved learning methods might not need to see the whole internet five times to learn a concept, clearly suggesting less training data could suffice.

r002.rationale: It points to algorithmic and software improvements, but does not predict superintelligence through software self-optimization alone; it allows that radical improvements may require new hardware.

r003.rationale: It mentions better software and architectures, but does not identify rebuilding the software stack from the ground up.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think the argument assumes that getting from AGI to superintelligence means continuing to scale up the same kinds of models in the same kinds of ways. And that’s not necessarily what happens once you have an AI that can do research as well as a human AI researcher.

At that point, you can apply the intelligence you already have to improving the algorithms. Can you learn more from less data? Can you reason more effectively with the same amount of computation? Can you reorganize the system so that you don’t need to retrain this enormous network every time you want to improve something? There’s no reason to think our current approaches are anywhere near the limit of computational efficiency.

So you could have a substantial increase in intelligence running on the hardware that’s already there. And then that smarter system is working on the next improvement. That feedback loop doesn’t necessarily have to wait for a new semiconductor factory.

Now, physical constraints are real. If you want to build a billion robots or cover the planet with new computing infrastructure, that takes time. But that’s different from making a system substantially smarter than human beings. I don’t think we know exactly how fast that transition will be, but I wouldn’t count on chip manufacturing being the bottleneck that gives us a long, comfortable interval between AGI and superintelligence.

r001.rationale: It raises learning more from less data as a possible improvement, but does not clearly compare AGI’s training data needs with those of modern LLMs.

r002.rationale: It describes an AI improving its algorithms and system, then gaining substantial intelligence on existing hardware, which communicates software self-optimization without new hardware.

r003.rationale: It mentions reorganizing the system to avoid retraining a large network, but does not identify rebuilding the software stack from the ground up.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think the assumption there is that getting from AGI to superintelligence requires vastly more hardware. And that’s not obvious to me. You may need a lot more computation if you’re just taking the same architecture and making it bigger. But an AGI can work on improving the architecture and the learning algorithms themselves.

Once you have a system that’s as good as a good human AI researcher, you can have it looking for more efficient ways to use the hardware you already have. It can improve its memory, its reasoning, the way it learns from experience. If those improvements make it better at doing AI research, then you have a feedback loop. You don’t necessarily have to wait for another semiconductor factory to be built for that loop to proceed.

Now, that doesn’t mean physical constraints disappear. If you want to build a billion robots, there’s manufacturing involved, and that takes time. And more computing power will certainly be useful. But I don’t see a compelling reason to assume that the hardware sufficient to support human-level general intelligence couldn’t also support something substantially smarter, running better software. So hardware could slow some aspects of the process without being the bottleneck on the intelligence itself.

r002.rationale: It says AGI could improve its architecture and learning algorithms, creating a feedback loop that makes it substantially smarter on the same hardware without waiting for more chips.

r003.rationale: It mentions improving architecture and algorithms but does not identify rebuilding the software stack from the ground up.
